title: Push it away
hookLine: how easy to push away a troubling thought and be at peace at once (Meditations 5.2)

lines: MARCUS IN BED, NOT GETTING UP.
A CLAIM THAT SOUNDS TOO EASY.
cards: Book five of the Meditations opens with Marcus arguing with himself in bed one morning, trying to get up. If you've ever hit snooze, you know that entry. The next one is shorter, and stranger.
It claims you can push a troubling thought away and be at peace, right away. If you've ever lain awake replaying a conversation, you might laugh. Easy?

teach.h: HOW EASY TO PUSH IT AWAY.
teach.b: How easy it is, Marcus writes, to push away and wipe out every impression that is troubling or out of place, and at once to be in perfect calm.
The Greek word for that calm, galene, is the word for a sea gone flat after wind. What's he pushing? Not the event, not the facts.

teach.h: PUSH THE IMPRESSION, NOT THE FACT.
teach.b: The impression: the first picture the mind paints, before you've agreed to it. Something happens, and an impression arrives saying this is terrible. You haven't yet said yes.
The push happens in that gap. Why easy?

teach.h: EASY AS PUTTING DOWN A CUP.
teach.b: The way putting down a cup is easy. The motion is small. What's hard is noticing you're holding it.
Often we don't keep a troubling thought on purpose; we just forget it's in our hand. And he's honest about the limits.

teach.h: FOR THE EVERYDAY, NOT THE GRIEF.
teach.b: Marcus isn't describing grief, or serious anxiety, or anything a person should face rather than push down. Those need time, people, and sometimes a doctor.
He means the everyday stuff: the stray irritation, the imagined argument, the small dread that floats in while you're doing the dishes.
For those, the first move is to set them down and see if you even need to pick them back up. Often you don't. And when you do need to think it through, you can choose a better time than 2am.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes practice Meditations 5.2 with small, everyday troubling thoughts, noticing them and setting them down; serious grief or anxiety is met in other ways.

o: the calm of a sea gone flat after the wind
a deep sleep that comes after a long, hard day
the Greek word for a storm building out at sea

games.q: push it away — tap the pairs.
p: a sea gone flat after wind
the first picture the mind paints

s: Marcus says to push away grief and serious fears
his point fits the everyday troubling thought, not grief or illness.
book five opens with Marcus trying to get out of bed
Marcus pushes away the impression, not the facts
the push happens in the gap before you agree to the first picture.

games.q: you're doing dishes and an imaginary argument with a coworker starts up in your head. what fits Meditations 5.2?
o: notice it, and set it down.
play it out to the end, to win.
text the coworker about it now.
games.why: Marcus says it's easy to push away an impression like that and be at once in calm: the hard part is noticing it.

practice: Let one small troubling thought come up, an irritation or a what-if, and feel it as a cup you're holding.
On the next out-breath, set it down beside you, not thrown, just set down, and see if the water inside you goes a little flatter. If it comes back, set it down again.

wordCard.voice: Galene, the Greek word for a sea gone flat, is what Marcus says follows when a troubling impression is pushed away. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'calm of the sea': the stillness Marcus says follows when a troubling impression is pushed away.

carryVoice: Your line: a sea gone flat. Most small troubles are cups we forgot we were holding. Day five hundred sixty-three, done.
